# Kurz language design

Status: brainstorm record, 2026-10-01 to 2026-11-02. Everything under "Decided" was chosen by the owner during the session. Anything marked *assumed* was proposed and not objected to, but never explicitly confirmed. A marker that carries the date of a review names a reading proposed after that review; it stands as assumed until the owner confirms or refuses it by number in a round. A marker *(proposed: ...)* inside a decided statement names a reading that the owner's answer did not reach; it is no decision, and a design round asks about it by the id of the reference rule that carries it. On 2026-10-02 the owner accepted, as one batch, the details the language reference had filled in to write its cases: the six that the question named are recorded as decided, the rest as *assumed*. Keyword spellings in code samples are illustrative unless listed in the syntax section.

## 1. Identity and goals

- Name: **Kurz**. Source files: `.kz`.
- Syntax in the spirit of C#.
- Main selling point: do as much as possible with as little code as possible.
- General purpose. Primary target: highly scalable, horizontally scalable backend systems.
- Games are a target, but the language gets no game-specific features.
- Should run on microcontrollers (Arduino, ESP32 class) without being designed for them. Consequence: the runtime is pay-per-use. A program that uses no actors links no scheduler.
- Compiled to native code, as fast as C, optimized for each target platform.
- A mechanism of Kurz is designed by first taking how Rust does it, and putting the developer experience and the distributed idea on top of that (the owner, 2026-10-20, round 16, in the owner's words: "i want to do it like rust/c for maximum performance, always when implementing smth for kurz check mainly how rust does it then apply our heavy developer experience and distributed idea on top of it"; against a mechanism chosen for the developer experience first; the cost is that a feature of the developer experience is paid for in the forms Rust pays it in and not by work on the hot path: the line of a crash and a trace cost the walk and the reads at the crash, as Rust pays for a backtrace when it is asked for (checked 2026-10-20: the Rust standard library's documentation of `std::backtrace`, which captures a backtrace at the point it is asked for), and the executable's size in every build, its unwind tables, its symbol names and the file and the line each raising site carries, while a release build keeps the line tables only under an option of the build, without which a stack overflow and a primitive's raise name no line there, and on Windows the tables and the names are a second file to ship beside the executable, without which a crash names no line (sections 2 and 6)); an internal form may leave Rust's where it measures faster with identical results, the code naming Rust's form and the measured reason it differs (the owner, 2026-11-01, "Allow, faster wins", against "Allow this one only", at the cost of a question to the owner for each such case, and against "Keep Rust's form", at the cost of 72 ms on a bench of 1 MiB of mixed text read 200 times by `string.FromUtf8`, the slower check pull request 154 left staying; the cost is a runtime that drifts from Rust's code, so that Rust's source no longer explains every loop) *(assumed: that any other departure from Rust's way is a question to the owner, as the reading of the owner's "always"; that C counts where Rust follows C, for the performance of both, as the reading of the owner's "rust/c" and "for maximum performance"; that the owner's "distributed idea" is the model of section 6 (decided there, with the assumptions its markers name) and section 7 (decided there); and the store of the line before every call of round 15, which section 6 (decided there) drops for the line tables, as an instance of the mechanism the principle is set against, which the record names and the owner did not; each proposed with this record and not put to the owner)*.
- The developer experience and the meaning of a program come from C#, made better where C# is weak; the performance and the memory safety come from Rust; and the distributed model comes from Elixir (the owner, 2026-10-29, in the owner's words: "generally the language will be: developer experience and semantics from c# but even better, performance memory safte and all that from rust, and elixir distributed stuff"). *(assumed: that it sharpens the line above, so that a mechanism starts from Rust's and what a program means starts from C#'s, the reading of the owner's "semantics from c#" beside round 16's "check mainly how rust does it", proposed with this record and not put to the owner)*
- Memory safety is proven by the compiler, not found by best-effort analysis. *(assumed)*
- The size of the language is counted, not capped: a gate prints the count of the core words, of the reference's rules and of its error ids on every change, and each question of a design round says what a new rule adds (the owner, 2026-10-30, "Printed counts", against no measure, at the cost that growth is seen only by reading, and against a budget of rules, at the cost that a good rule can be refused for the count; the cost is a small tool and one line per question). The reference's lint prints the count of its rules and of its error ids on every run; no tool prints the count of the core words, and the questions of a design round carry no line on what a new rule adds: that part is not built.

## 2. Toolchain

- The compiler emits LLVM IR directly. Going through C source is not wanted. LLVM as a build-time dependency is acceptable.
- The emitted IR is compiled and linked by the `clang` of an LLVM release that the machine or the image that builds has: the compiler accepts one major release of LLVM, the one it pins, and tries `clang-<major>` for that major, where the distribution installs such names, then `clang`, where the installer gives that name alone, as the LLVM installer on Windows does (checked 2026-10-15 in the `bin` directory that installer fills: `clang.exe`, and no `clang-<major>.exe`), both on the path, and on Windows then `clang.exe` in that directory, `%ProgramFiles%\LLVM\bin`, for a machine on which the installer did not add that directory to the path (the owner, 2026-10-21, round 20, "Path + installer dir", as Rust's compiler finds the linker of its MSVC targets through the installation of Visual Studio and not on the path alone (checked 2026-10-21: rustc's choice of a linker, `get_linker` in `rustc_codegen_ssa`, which asks the `find-msvc-tools` crate for `link.exe`, which takes the tools on the path of a developer command prompt and otherwise looks for the newest installation of Visual Studio), against the path alone, at the cost that a user on Windows who did not let the installer add LLVM to the path is told that clang is not there, and against the path and a variable that names the clang, at the cost of one more name to set wrong, which the gate tests; the cost is a third place to look, and that of two installs the one on the path wins, while a refusal of it names the place it was found in) *(assumed: that the first of the places that holds a clang, three on Windows and two elsewhere, gives the one taken and that a refusal of it ends the search, the reading of that answer's cost, under which the install on the path wins, said back to the owner on 2026-10-21 and not objected to)*, asks the one it found for its version and refuses it when its major is not the pinned one, on every machine (the owner, 2026-10-21, round 17, "One pinned release", Rust's way as the question named it, rustc shipping one LLVM, against the last two majors, at the cost that the emitter handles their differences in IR text and CI tests both, and against a minimum and up, at the cost that a newer release runs untested while nobody has tried it; the cost is that moving to a newer LLVM is a release of the compiler); Apple's clang, whose version is Apple's own and names no LLVM release, is refused whatever number its answer names (the owner, 2026-10-23, "Refuse it outright", as Apple numbers the clang it ships apart from LLVM's releases (checked 2026-10-23: the table of toolchain versions in the English Wikipedia's article on Xcode, under which Apple clang 17.0.0 is built from LLVM 19.1.4 and 19.1.5, and Apple clang 21.0.0 from LLVM 21.1.6), against a table from Apple's versions to the LLVM releases they are built from, which Apple publishes no list of, at the cost of a table that ages, and against reading Apple's number as a release, under which a refusal names a number that is no LLVM release and an Apple clang of the pinned number passes whatever LLVM it is built from; the cost is that a Mac with Apple's clang alone, one built from the pinned major among them, builds nothing, and LLVM's clang has to stand ahead of it on the path); the compiler's gate must print the version the compiler found and fail when the compiler refused it or found none, a requirement this record puts on the gate; the gate learns that version from the command, running `kurz --version` and printing its output, the compiler's version, the major of LLVM the compiler pins and the clang it found with that clang's version, and failing where the command ends with an exit code other than zero, which it does where it refused that clang or found none (the owner, 2026-10-21, round 20, "kurz --version", as `rustc -vV` prints, among its lines, the version of the LLVM it was built with, which rustc ships, so that it has no other to refuse (checked 2026-10-21: rustc's driver, which prints its version under `-V` and, under `-vV`, also the version of its backend after its own lines, and the LLVM backend's `print_version`, which prints `LLVM version:` with the major, the minor and the patch, read and not run), against a test of the compiler's suite that prints it, at the cost that a user cannot ask for it and that the gate parses the log of a test; the cost is one more option of the command, whose output lines the gate reads), so that on a machine with no clang that the compiler takes, `kurz --version` ends with a failure, which a caller that asks it for the version alone, to learn whether `kurz` is there, reads as a failure of the command, a cost the question did not name *(assumed: that the command writes those lines on standard output, said back to the owner on 2026-10-21 and not objected to)*; `kurz --version` writes them on one line, `kurz <version> (LLVM <major>, clang <release> at <path>)`, and `kurz --version --verbose` on lines of their own, `kurz <version>`, `LLVM version: <major>`, `clang: <path>` and `clang version: <release>` (the owner, 2026-10-23, "One line, like rustc --version", as `rustc -V` writes one line and `rustc -vV` its lines (checked 2026-10-21, above), against those four lines under `--version` alone, at the cost that a caller that wants the parts reads them out of one line; the cost is a second option of the command); before a failure `--version` writes the line without the clang, `kurz <version> (LLVM <major>)`, and `--version --verbose` its first two lines, and `--verbose` stands before or after `--version`, as rustc takes `-v` and `-V` in either order (the owner, 2026-10-23, "Keep them", the readings of that answer said back to the owner, against no output on standard output before a failure, at the cost that a failed run tells a caller no pinned major; the cost is a line on standard output that a caller which asks for the version alone takes for an answer unless it reads the exit code): the pinned major is the newest stable major release of LLVM at the time of the pin, and this record names no number, so that moving to another changes the number the compiler names alone, and the emitter where the release's IR text differs (the owner, 2026-10-21, round 17, "Newest stable", against the major the distribution of the CI image ships, at the cost of an older LLVM; A requirement this record puts on this repository's CI is an image the repository builds itself, with the pinned release of LLVM from those packages, pushes to GitHub's container registry and builds again when the pin moves, an image the job `gates` runs in, while the Windows job, which no such image serves, installs that release on every run from a cache, so that an image not built again after the pin moved holds a clang of another major, which the compiler refuses, a red run (above) (the owner, 2026-10-21, round 20, "Own Linux image", as Rust's own repository runs its Linux jobs in images it builds from its own source and its Windows jobs install their tools on every run (checked 2026-10-21: the rustc dev guide's chapter on CI, under which every job but those on macOS and Windows runs in a Docker image of the repository's own, built from `src/ci/docker` and cached on GitHub's container registry, and `src/ci/scripts/install-clang.sh` in its repository, which its CI runs and which on Windows downloads the LLVM installer of a pinned release and unpacks it, with no cache, each time it runs), against an install of that release on every run on both systems, from a cache, which the question named Rust's CI, at the cost of a minute or two at each miss of the cache, a download from outside the image, and a change to this record's "not on every run"; ## 3. Memory

- No lifetimes, no borrow annotations, no global garbage collector.
- Immutable by default. Immutable data cannot form reference cycles, so compiler-inserted reference counting is enough, and most counting is optimized away at compile time.
- Mutable state lives inside exactly one actor. Each actor has its own heap. When an actor dies its whole heap is freed at once. A big value that is shared between actors lives outside these heaps (section 6).
- There is **no cycle collector**. A possible reference cycle is a compile error.
  - The rule is judged by types, over the whole program: a class may not reach itself through strong fields when one field on that path is `mut`. Values cannot contain themselves (section 4), so the rule only ever applies to classes.
  - `weak` means "I point at this but do not keep it alive". A weak reference is nullable and becomes null when its target is freed. It is the same idea as `WeakReference<T>` in C#. A weak type always shows its `?`: `weak Node?` (the owner, 2026-10-02). A read of a `weak T?` place gives a strong `T?`, which holds the target as a temporary holds it, to the end of its statement, and longer where the read is stored: `k = p.Keeper` holds the target while `k` lives, and a `T?` parameter takes the read as it is, as Swift reads a `weak var` (the owner, 2026-11-01, "A strong T?, held", against a read that stays `weak T?` until `?.`, `??`, a test or a member makes a `T?` of it, as Rust's `Weak::upgrade` and C#'s `TryGetTarget` give one, at the cost of a word or a test at every use; the cost is that a variable that stores the read keeps the target alive as long as the variable lives). A `weak T?` type stands wherever a type stands, a variable, a parameter, a return type, a map's value and a union's case among them, as Rust's `Weak<T>` is an ordinary type (the owner, 2026-11-01, "Anywhere a type stands", against a field and a list's item alone, every other place an error with an id of its own, at the cost of that id and of a reference that a function can neither take nor give; the cost is more places to check and test); what a nullable type written as a case of a union is stays open (section 14), a `weak T?` among them. A `weak T?` field of a `data` type compares by its target's identity, as Rust's `Weak::ptr_eq`: two values are equal where the field reaches the same instance, and a freed target reads as null, so two freed references are equal and a freed one equals an explicit `null`; a `data` type keeps its derived `==` with a `weak T?` field (the owner, 2026-11-02, #110, comment 6580085338, against refusing such a field, as Rust cannot derive `PartialEq` for a struct that holds a `Weak`, and against listing it under Open; the cost is that the value's `==` changes when the target is freed). A `weak T?` is no key of a `Map`, and neither is a type that reaches one through what `==` compares by content, a field of a `data` type, an item of a list or a nullable, while a `weak` behind a class that compares by identity does not count, since such a class hashes by its address: such a key type is a compile error with an id of its own, since a key whose target is freed changes what it equals and hashes to, and the map would lose it, as it would a key whose `mut` field is assigned (the owner, 2026-11-02, #110, comments 6580085338 and 6580137405, as Rust's `Weak` is not `Hash` and its derived `Hash` fails on a struct that holds one, against listing it under Open and against refusing only a bare `weak` key; the cost is that a map keyed by a weak target is a structure of its own, as C#'s `ConditionalWeakTable` is). The error's id is `weak-key`, and it stands at the line that writes the key type, as `mutable-key` does *(assumed: the id and the line proposed with this record; the answer asked for an id of its own)*. A `weak` map value stays as above.
  - Between different types, `weak` on the back-pointer is enough: `Customer` holds its orders, `Order` points back `weak`. A class that reaches itself through a strong `mut` field is rejected even with a `weak` back-pointer, because `a.children.Add(b)` followed by `b.children.Add(a)` closes a ring through the children alone.
  - Only `mut` fields can close a cycle, so with immutable-by-default the error is rare.
  - A `mut` field of interface type could hold any implementer; the compiler needs the whole program to judge it. A field of function type, `mut` or not, is judged the same way: the lambda it holds can capture any class instance, so the field counts as reaching every class whose instance a lambda it can hold captures (below), and the `mut` field that closes the ring can be the function field or any other field on the path; a button that stores a handler that reads the button is a cycle (the owner, 2026-10-03, against a weak capture inside stored lambdas and against forbidding such a capture; that a field without `mut` counts too follows from a ring the review showed through one, *(assumed)*). What a lambda captures is read as a field of its type: a `weak` reference it captures reaches no class, as a `weak` field reaches none; a value of a type parameter reaches the classes of the type argument every call of its function names or infers, through the type parameters of a generic caller in turn, as the copy for each list of type arguments holds them (section 4); and a method taken as a value captures its instance, as a C# delegate keeps its target (the owner, 2026-11-02, #110, comment 6573113786, R9a to R9c: against counting a captured `weak` reference as strong, at the cost of the escape a `weak` field gives, against every class of the program for a type parameter, at the cost of an error for every ring through a field of function type once one such lambda exists, and against a method value that captures nothing, at the cost of the leak R2 refuses; the cost is that the checker reads every call of a generic function, and of the generic functions that call it, before it judges a field). The field counts only the lambdas whose type it can hold, and the lambdas a function value such a lambda captures can be, every lambda where a type on the way names a type parameter, since a field of a function type holds only a function of a type it can hold (the owner, 2026-11-04, #110, comment 6643368937, answering comment 6624472418, against every lambda of the program, which would make every program in which a lambda captures an `HttpResponse`, whose streamed body is such a field, a cycle, and against the field set once without `mut`, which needs constructors in a class body; the cost is the checker's match of each lambda's type). *(assumed: the count is transitive, the lambdas a function value of a counted lambda can be counted in turn until no lambda is added, and the types on the way are the lambda's own type, which makes it count for every field where it names a type parameter, and the type of a value a counted lambda captures, or of a function value such a value holds, which makes every lambda of the program count where it names one, as the checker takes them; the cost is a count the checker repeats until no lambda is added, and rings that are wider and harder to foresee: one lambda whose type names a type parameter counts for every field, and one counted capture of a value whose type names one makes every lambda of the program count)* The cost is not local: once a class has a field of function type, any lambda the field counts, anywhere in the program, that captures an instance of that class, or of a class that holds one, makes it an error, and the lambda can sit in another file. An event handler escapes the error only in a program in which no lambda the button's field counts captures the button's class: through an interface (which must not hold the button), or by receiving the button as a parameter.

Koka's purely functional red-black tree, updated in place this way, ran 42 million inserts within 10% of C++ `std::map` ([Perceus, MSR-TR-2020-42](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/perceus-tr-v1.pdf)); a later paper measured it 19% faster on one CPU and about equal on another ([Frame Limited Reuse, MSR-TR-2021-30](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2021/11/flreuse-tr.pdf)).

data Tree(int Key, Tree? Left, Tree? Right)

root.Key = 9

class Scene { mut Map<int, Node> nodes }      // owns every node
class Node {
    mut List<weak Node?> children
    mut weak Node? parent
}
```

## 4. Types and paradigm

- Static typing with inference.
- Immutable by default; `mut` marks what may change.
- **Values.** `data`, collections, strings and numbers are values (the owner chose this as "probably" on 2026-10-01; the cycle rule of section 3 and the `mut` parameters below were chosen afterwards and build on it):
  - Without `mut`, nothing reachable through a variable changes. With `mut`, it changes in place. The guarantee stops at a class instance: its `mut` fields change through every reference to it, whatever holds the reference (the class bullet below), so what a variable reaches through an instance is not covered. *(assumed: the qualification; it follows from the owner's choice on `mut` fields)*
  - Assigning or passing a value copies it in meaning. In practice the storage is shared until one side writes, and a write happens in place when nobody else holds the value, but for a write into a block of a `data` value, which copies the block (below). Where the compiler cannot prove that, a counter check precedes the write. The counter of a list is the count of the list values that hold its storage, which a copy raises and the end of a holder lowers, at the end of its scope, at an assignment over it and where the value that holds it ends, and the storage is freed when the count reaches zero, as Swift's `Array` counts its storage and copies it at a write while another array holds it (the owner, 2026-10-24, "Full counting now", against a count that only grows, under which nothing is freed and a list shared once is copied at its next write after the other holder is gone, and against a copy of the list at every copy, as C++ copies a `std::vector` by value, every item at every assignment and nothing freed; the cost is the count in every list, a change of it at every copy and every end of a holder, and code at each of those places for every variable, field and union case that holds a list, which the option named as "the largest change to the emitter, with drop points for every variable, field and union"). A string is counted as a list's storage is: a string made while the program runs holds its bytes in a block that holds, in front of them, the count of the values that hold the block, the count of its bytes and the room it was given, 16 bytes, laid out as a list of bytes lays out its block, so that `s.Bytes` shares it (below), as Rust's `Arc<str>` holds its counts in front of the text in one allocation (checked 2026-10-29 with Rust 1.82: an `Arc<str>` is the 16 bytes of an address and a length, and `Arc::from` of a `String` copies the text into the allocation of the counts); a copy raises the count, the end of a holder lowers it where a list's count is lowered, and the block is freed when the count reaches zero; a string never changes (below), so no write copies a block *(assumed: the block in front of the bytes, its 16 bytes and the counts and the room among them, proposed with this record and not put to the owner)*. A literal holds no block, the empty literal among them, and is never freed, and a string tells the two apart by the highest bit of the 64-bit word that holds its count of bytes, which the limit of the largest `int` (below) leaves free, so that a copy and the end of a literal read no memory (the owner, 2026-10-29, "Bit in the count", as Swift marks a literal string immortal in the highest bit of its 16-byte value (checked 2026-10-29: `StringObject.swift` in Swift's standard library, "b63: isImmortal: Should the Swift runtime skip ARC", "Large strings can sometimes be immortal, e.g. literals") and as Rust's `Cow<'static, str>` keeps its tag in values the capacity of a `String` never takes (checked 2026-10-29 with Rust 1.82: a `Cow<str>` takes the 24 bytes of a `String`), against a count in front of every literal too, in the executable, whose value means never freed, as Swift's statically allocated objects hold one, at the cost of 16 bytes for each literal and a read of memory at every copy and end of one, and against a test of the address against the constants of the executable, at the cost of two comparisons with symbols that differ for each target and linker; the cost is a mask at every read of the count of bytes and the 16 bytes in front of every string made while the program runs). - Integer overflow wraps silently in release builds. Around that:
  - Compile errors for constant expressions that overflow, implicit narrowing (`long` into `int`) and mixing `uint` or `ulong` with a signed type (below). A constant expression under `+%`, `-%` or `*%` folds to the wrapped value instead, as the operator promises for every value, `2147483647 +% 1` to `-2147483648`; a conversion to an integer type written on a constant that does not fit its target, `byte(300)`, is the overflow error, as C# refuses a constant cast that does not fit (the owner, 2026-10-09, against both being the error, under which a checksum written on literals does not compile, and against both computing, under which `byte(300)` is `44` and a value is lost without a word; the cost is a constant folder that knows two kinds of operator). An overflowing constant expression is the error for the integer types and `decimal` alone: one of `float` or `double` folds to the value IEEE 754 gives it, an infinity or NaN included, as C# folds it. A literal whose value lies outside the range of the type it takes is the error whatever that type, a duration (below) included: `1e400` or `3.5e38f` is the error, as C# refuses such a literal, and one that rounds to zero or to a subnormal is that value, as there. A constant fits the target of a written integer conversion when its value, the fraction dropped, lies in the target's range: `int(2.5)` is `2`, and `int(1e10)`, `int(1.0 / 0.0)` and a NaN are the overflow error (the owner, 2026-10-10, confirming the reading proposed after the review of round 13). A written conversion to a floating-point type folds as IEEE 754 has it, to an infinity beyond the range and with rounding, never the error (the owner, 2026-10-10). A constant expression of a time type, which counts nanoseconds in an integer, is the error as an integer one is; a written conversion to `decimal` fits when the value, rounded to `decimal`'s precision, lies in its range, and `decimal(1e30)` is the error (the owner, 2026-10-11, confirming the reading proposed after the review of round 14).

  - An integer literal is an `int`, or a `long` when its value does not fit, or a `ulong` when a `long` does not, without C#'s step through `uint` (the owner, 2026-10-10, confirming the reference's reading L10 and its ladder); where an integer type is written or expected it takes that type *(assumed)*, and is the overflow error below when the value does not fit it; where the written type is no number type, `string s = 300`, the literal is the error for a value of one type where another is required, as any value is *(assumed: it follows from the type error of this section and was not put to the owner)*. A written or expected type reaches every literal of a constant expression, so `long big = 2147483647 + 1` is a `long`, and a literal that is one operand of an operator whose other operand has a type takes that type, so the `1` of `u + 1` with a `uint` is a `uint` and the `100` of `sbyte low = -100` is an `sbyte` (the owner, 2026-10-10, confirming the reference's reading L17, which round 13 had not asked about; C# converts the constant `int` instead, which Kurz cannot do across signedness). The promotion of narrow operands below is for the operands of a run-time operation. A constant expression is folded in the type its literals take, one operation at a time, each operation by the rule of its own operator: under `+ - * / %` an operation whose result leaves an integer or `decimal` type is the constant-overflow error, where a floating-point one folds to its IEEE 754 value (above), and under `+%`, `-%` and `*%` it wraps in that type. So `sbyte low = -100` and `byte c = 200 + 50` compile, `byte c = 200 + 100` is the error, and so is `byte c = 200 + 100 - 100`, whose result would fit but whose first sum does not; `byte b = 255 +% 1` is `0`, and `2147483647 + 1 +% 0`, with no written type and so in `int`, is the error at the `+`. A literal that does not fit the type it takes is the constant-overflow error wherever it stands: `byte c = 300`, never an `int` narrowed, and `b + 300` with a `byte` `b`, whose `300` takes `byte` by the sentence above, as much as `sum +% 300` (below); the cost is that `b * 1000` on a `byte` is written `int(b) * 1000`. Kurz departs from C# here, where a constant expression has the type of its operands, `int` for `2147483647 + 1` whatever the written type, and overflows there (the owner, 2026-10-10, confirming the reading proposed after the review of round 13). The target of a written conversion reaches the integer literals inside it, so `long(2147483647 + 1)` is `2147483648`, while a fraction or exponent literal inside it keeps its own type and the conversion applies to the folded value, so `float(1e300)` is an infinity (above) and `int(2.5)` is `2` (the owner, 2026-10-11, confirming the reading proposed after the review of round 14); a `-` written directly before a literal, with no operand before the `-`, belongs to the literal, so `sbyte x = -128` and `int x = -2147483648` compile and `n-1` stays a subtraction; a written floating-point or `decimal` type reaches integer literals as well, so `double d = 1 / 2` is `0.5`, where C# divides the integers first; a fraction or exponent literal beside an integer operand keeps its type, and the integer operand widens to it, so `b + 1.5` with a `byte` is a `double`; and literals of different types in one constant expression fold in the type `+` would find for them at run time (the owner, 2026-10-10). Under a written or expected type every literal takes it first, so `float f = 1 + 2.5` is `3.5` as a `float` and `float f = 1e300` the overflow error of a literal outside its type's range, and a fraction literal under a written integer type, `int i = 1 + 2.5`, is the error for a value of one type where another is required, as `string s = 300` is (the owner, 2026-10-11, confirming the reading proposed after the review of round 14).
  - A narrower integer becomes a wider one without a word when the wider type holds every value of the narrower, as in C#: within one signedness, and across it where C# widens (`byte` into `short`, `int` and `long`, `ushort` into `int` and `long`, `uint` into `long`); every integer type becomes `float`, `double` or `decimal` without a word, rounded to the nearest value the type holds where it does not hold every value, as in C#, and that rounding is not a loss in the sense of the conversion rule below; a signed type never becomes unsigned without a word (the owner, 2026-10-03, against widening within one signedness only, under which `int x = b` with a `byte` needs `int(b)`). The cost: `b + i` with a `byte` and an `int` is an `int`, and `float f = i` rounds without a word where `float(i)` is checked. Where the two rules meet: an operation finds its common type as C# does, except where C# joins a signed with an unsigned operand through `long` or refuses the pair, which is `uint` or `ulong` with a signed type; there Kurz reports the error for mixing signed with unsigned. So `u + i` with a `uint` and an `int` is the error where C# computes a `long`, while `sb + b` with an `sbyte` and a `byte` is an `int` and `u + b` with a `uint` and a `byte` is a `uint`, as there. The error looks at the two operand types as written, before any promotion: a `byte` or a `ushort` beside a `uint` becomes a `uint` and beside a `ulong` a `ulong`, as C#'s binary numeric promotion makes it, not an `int` first (the promotion bullet below). (the owner, 2026-10-04, against C#'s `long` for `uint` with `int`) Where a union is required, a value that is no case of it stands there when it widens into exactly one of its cases, so a `byte` stands where `int | string` is required; one that would widen into two of them, a `byte` where `short | int` is required, is the error for a value of one type where another is required, and a conversion such as `short(b)` picks the case, by the same rule that makes a call that fits two functions through widening an error (section 8) (the owner, 2026-10-21, against the narrowest case, under which the `byte` becomes a `short` by C#'s better-conversion rule, and against no widening into unions, under which the value must be one of the cases exactly, as Rust widens nothing implicitly; the cost is a conversion at such places). A value that is one of the cases, a `data` value among them, is that case, and no other fit by widening or derivation is looked for, so a `short` where `short | int` is required is a `short`, and a `User` where `User | Person` is required, with `User : Person`, is a `User` (the owner, 2026-10-21, against a value that would also go to another case by widening or derivation being the error for a value of one type where another is required, as two fits are, under which that `User` is that error too; C#'s better-conversion rule prefers the identity conversion, and Rust has only the exact fit; the cost is that adding a case to a union can change without a word which case an existing value goes to, as a `User` goes to `Person` where `int | Person` is required and to `User` where `int | Person | User` is, while under the option turned down that addition is a compile error; the owner kept this answer with that cost shown on 2026-10-21). A union with exactly one number case, a case of a number type (an integer type, `float`, `double` or `decimal`), reaches a number literal, an integer literal or one with a fraction or an exponent, as a written type does, so `byte | string x = 5` makes the `5` a `byte`; where it has two or more number cases the literal has its own type, so `byte | short x = 5`, whose `int` widens into neither case, is that error too, and `byte(5)` picks the case (the owner, 2026-10-21, against every number case the literal fits reaching it, with two fits the error, under which `byte | short x = 300` is a `short` and the case depends on the literal's value, and against the literal's own type even beside one number case, under which `byte | string x = 5` needs a conversion; the cost is a conversion at such places, as for a literal whose own type would widen into two cases). The union's one time case, a case of a time type (`duration`, `timestamp`, `longduration` or `longtimestamp`), reaches a duration literal as a written type does, whatever number cases the union has, so `int | duration d = 5days` makes the literal a `duration` and `duration | string d = 106752days` is the overflow error; with two or more time cases the literal keeps its own type, a `duration`, or a `longduration` when its value does not fit one (the owner, 2026-10-21, against the literal's own type always, under which that second example is the error for a value of one type where another is required; the cost is the same conversion at such places as for a number literal).
  - A conversion on purpose is the type's name used as a function: `int(value)`. A conversion that loses the value behaves as overflow does: it wraps in a release build and throws in a test build (the owner, 2026-10-02), but for a time value narrowed into the 64-bit pair, which throws in every build (above), and for a conversion into `decimal`, which throws in every build as well (below); this is for a value the program computes, since a conversion to an integer type written on a constant that does not fit is the compile error above, and one to a floating-point type folds as section 4 says. From a `double`, `float` or `decimal` source into an integer type, a dropped fraction is no loss: `int(2.5)` is `2`, toward zero, as in C#. A value outside the target's range, an infinity and NaN lose the value: a test build throws, and a release build gives the target's largest or smallest value for an out-of-range value and an infinity, and `0` for NaN (the owner, 2026-10-03, against wrapping the integer part as an integer source wraps, and against counting a dropped fraction as a loss). The saturation is Kurz's own definition: C# leaves the result unspecified, .NET saturates on every platform since .NET 9, and for a `decimal` source C# throws in every build. So "wraps" describes an integer source and "saturates" a floating-point or `decimal` one. Between the floating-point types and `decimal` the IEEE 754 rules of C# hold: a `double` into a `float` rounds and becomes an infinity beyond the range, NaN stays NaN and an infinity stays an infinity *(assumed: the `float` and `double` targets, which the question of 2026-10-03 did not name)*. Into `decimal`, which has neither, NaN, an infinity and a value beyond its range raise the overflow exception in every build, a release build too, as C# throws for them (the owner, 2026-10-28, "Raise in every build", against saturating in a release build and throwing in a test build as an integer target does, which this bullet assumed before; the cost is a release program that ends with an error line instead of a clamped amount). A `double` becomes its exact binary value rounded half to even at the largest scale up to 28 whose digits fit `decimal`'s 96 bits, its zeros at the end removed down to the scale 0: `decimal(0.1)` is `0.1000000000000000055511151231` (the owner, 2026-10-28, "Exact binary value", against the shortest digits that read back as the same `double`, `0.1`, as the Rust crate rust_decimal's `from_f64` gives them, and against the 15 significant digits C# keeps; the cost is surprising digits for almost every `double`; rust_decimal's `from_f64_retain` comes near it and differs in the last digits, `123.456` giving `123.45600000000000306954461843` where the exact value rounds to `123.45600000000000306954461848`, checked on 2026-10-28 with rust_decimal 1.36) *(assumed: the rounding half to even, the largest scale whose digits fit and the zeros removed at the end, readings of the option's "rounded to 28 digits")*; that rounding is no loss. A `float` becomes the `double` that holds it exactly, and then that *(assumed: the answer named the exact binary value, which the `double` holds; C# keeps 7 significant digits of a `float`)*. A zero that comes of the conversion has no sign, `decimal(-0.0)` included *(assumed: the reading of the answer "None, as rust_decimal", under which only the unary `-` gives a zero its sign)*. A `decimal` becomes a `double` as C# computes it: the low 64 bits of its 96-bit integer as a `double`, plus its high 32 bits times 2^64 as a `double`, divided by the `double` nearest to 10 to the power of its scale, as .NET's `VarR8FromDec` computes it, so `double(1m / 3m)` is `0.33333333333333337` (the owner, 2026-10-28, "As C# computes it", against the nearest `double`, `0.3333333333333333`; the cost is a last bit that can differ from the nearest `double`), and a `float` as that `double` rounded, as C# computes it *(assumed)*.

## 5. Outcomes and errors

The language enforces the C# `OneOf<>` pattern: every method declares every outcome that can happen under normal use.

- The return type is a union. The **first case is the success case**. ```
data User(int Id, string Name, string? Email)
data NotFound

actor UserStore {
    mut users = Map<int, User>()

    pub User | NotFound Get(int id) => users[id] ?? NotFound
}

pub User | NotFound | Invalid Rename(UserStore store, int id, string name) {
    if name == "" { return Invalid }
    user = store.Get(id)                 // user is a User; NotFound went to the caller
    return user with { Name = name }
}

// keep all cases
User | NotFound result = store.Get(id)

match store.Get(id) {
    User u   => print(u.Name)
    NotFound => print("none")
}

// handle selected cases
user = store.Get(id) else { NotFound => User.Guest }                       // recover
user = store.Get(id) else { NotFound => return Invalid }                   // transform
user = store.Get(id) else { NotFound => throw }                            // cannot happen here
```

## 6. Concurrency

### Actors

An actor is an object with private state, its own heap and an inbox. In C# terms: a class with a private `Channel<T>` and one task looping over it, all written by the compiler.

- Nobody outside can touch its fields.
- Calls on an actor look like ordinary method calls. The compiler turns each into a message.
- An actor handles one message at a time, so there are no locks and no data races inside it.
- An idle actor costs no CPU and a few hundred bytes. Millions run on a handful of OS threads.
- There is no `async`/`await`. Every call looks synchronous; the runtime parks the actor while it waits.
- An actor parked in the middle of a call is a compiler-made state machine, built only for functions that can wait; the whole-program view knows which ones. All other code runs on the ordinary stack. *(assumed)*
- Messages from one actor to another arrive in the order they were sent. *(assumed)*
- A call waits for its result by default. `send` makes a call fire-and-forget: `send store.Add(user)`. *(Waiting by default is the reading of "the Elixir way" that was stated back to the owner.)*
- What may cross between actors: values (`data`, collections, strings, numbers), immutable class instances and actor references. A mutable class instance crosses only with an explicit word at the call: `copy` (the receiver gets a deep copy) or `move` (the sender's variable is dead afterwards, nothing is copied), and a send of one with neither is the compile error `send-needs-word`, whose id stands here as `move-reachable`'s does (below) *(assumed: the error's name, which no answer spelled)*. The region check below holds that two actors never reach the same mutable object, but for two exceptions of a server's stream that it does not see (section 12). The first is a hand-back: the read half comes back to the server at the end of the moved body that took it, and that body holds the only path into the half until its end and gives that path up before the half goes back, while the server holds the other half. The second is the state that the two halves of one connection share in their pair, which two actors can reach: a write, the one `100 Continue` that a body's first read writes on the server's write half, in the actor that reads, while no response has begun, where the server writes a response's head once the handler's call has returned, and with it the pair's flag, the time of the body's last read and the server's end of the body, each part read and written atomically and shared only between the two halves of one connection (the owner, 2026-11-07, issue 39, comment 6706852249, the pair as a whole, against keeping the exception to the flag alone with a message for each read, at the cost of a message per read on the body's path) *(assumed: the cost of the choice, an atomic write of the time of the body's last read at each read and more state shared between two actors, which `std/`'s code keeps right without the checker, the reading of the round of pull request 399, issue 39, comment 6724701136)*. The pair's one flag keeps the two writes apart, taken by an atomic test-and-set before either write (the owner, 2026-11-06, issue 39, comment 6682072588), and it holds one of four states: free, `100 Continue` under way, `100 Continue` written and a response begun. ### Scheduling

Switching between actors is cooperative by default: an actor gives up its core at actor calls and I/O. A runaway loop then costs one core, not the system, because other cores take over the waiting actors.

- An actor opts into stronger fairness after its name, where `per` sits as well. `yield checks`: the compiler inserts switch points at loop ends and function entry. `yield timer`: a timer interrupt switches the actor out.
- The compiler warns about a loop inside an actor that has no switch point and no provable end.

```
actor ReportBuilder yield checks { ... }
actor ReportBuilder yield timer { ... }
```

- The supervisor is whoever spawned the actor; no extra code. Explicit supervisor trees exist only for other policies.
