```
rows = attempt { Import(file) } else { Crashed c => return ImportFailed(c.Reason) }

w = spawn Worker(queue)                                   // default: restart fresh; too many crashes crash the spawner
w = spawn Worker(queue) on crash stop
w = spawn Worker(queue) on crash restart after 1s max 10 in 1min
w = spawn Worker(queue) on crash (c) {
    log("died: {c.Reason}")
    restart
}
```

### Deadlocks

Three layers, so that a hang cannot happen silently.

1. **Callbacks work.** Every call carries a chain ID. An actor waiting inside a chain lets in calls that belong to the same chain. `A.Save` waits on `B.Check`, which calls `A.Load`: this runs like a nested method call. Unrelated messages still wait.
2. **Compile error for loops of waiting calls between actor types**, analysed per method. `vouch` on the call overrides it and means "different instance, I vouch": `vouch c.Size()`. Exempt without override: a callback through a reference the caller passed in that same call.
3. **Instant runtime detection.** On every wait the runtime follows the wait line. If it leads back, one actor gets an exception immediately, naming both chains, and its supervisor restarts it.

Across machines, layer 3 sees chain loops but not crossing chains; those fall to the timeout.

A waiting actor finds its reply and the calls of its chain with no scan of its inbox: a call's reply goes to a one-shot slot made for that call, and a message whose chain ID names a chain its target waits in goes to a side slot as it is queued (the owner, 2026-10-30, "One-shot reply slot", as Tokio answers a request through a `oneshot` channel made for it, against a scan of the inbox at each wait, Erlang's selective receive, at the cost of a wait that grows with the queue; the cost is a lookup for each message queued and a small map for each waiting actor).

Side effect: the chain ID doubles as the trace ID of a trace the program starts, so log lines can carry it automatically. Each call and `send` carries beside it the span that made it, and the HTTP server and client carry the trace in `traceparent` (section 12, "Logging, tracing and metrics") (the owner, 2026-11-04, logging, tracing and metrics, Q4 (a), #274, comment 6643369246). A trace that comes in by `traceparent` travels beside the chain ID and does not become it: the chain ID stays the runtime's own, so that two requests that send one trace-id never share a chain (section 12, the owner, 2026-11-05, the chain ID, #274, comment 6657252063).

## 7. Distribution

- Built into the language and on by default. A compiler flag turns it off for single-machine targets such as ESP32.
- A call on an actor works unchanged whether the actor lives in this process or on another machine. Clustering, remote spawn and serialization are part of the runtime.
- **Network split**, applied to everything cluster-wide (singleton actors as well as jobs):
  1. The side holding the majority of machines runs it.
  2. On an exact tie no side holds a majority, and neither runs it: both stop their members ("Failures", below).
  3. If no side qualifies, the policy is per item: `skip` (default), or run on all sides with a developer-written `merge` block that is called with both results when the cluster heals. Whether such a side runs at all, where a side without a majority stops its members (item 2 and "Failures", below), stands open (section 14).
  - Kurz can compare and replay its own state only. Effects on the outside world (an email, a payment) cannot be merged.
- **Members.** Members connect on demand, and the cluster-wide directory of keyed actors (section 13) is split across them by consistent hashing over the list of members, as Orleans splits its directory of grains (the owner, 2026-10-30, "Consistent hash, Orleans", against a full mesh and a directory copied to every machine, as Erlang's `global`, at the cost of n² links and an agreement of the whole cluster for every new key, and against a directory service outside the program, as etcd, at the cost of that dependency and its availability; the cost is one more hop on a miss in the directory, a protocol of membership and a move of entries at each join). Every join and every leave goes through a log of the members that a majority of the current members agree on, as Raft keeps one, and the majority of the network split counts that set (the owner, 2026-10-30, "Raft membership", against a fixed list of members in `project.kz`, at the cost of a redeploy to grow the cluster, and against the last view each side saw, at the cost of two majorities after a join during a split; the cost is a consensus protocol in the runtime, and a join needs a majority up).
- **Failures.** Members send each other a heartbeat every second, and a phi-accrual failure detector reads them, as Akka's cluster reads them; a member unreachable for a set time, 20 s as in Akka's split brain resolver, is taken out of the log of the members by the side that holds the majority, and the side without it stops its members (the owner, 2026-10-30, "Phi accrual + majority, as Akka", against a fixed tick, as Erlang's, a tick every 15 s and `net_ticktime` 60 s, a `nodedown` and the program deciding, at the cost of 60 s to notice and a split brain left to the program; the cost is about 20 s for each split, and a side without a majority that stops) *(assumed: the detector's threshold and its other settings at Akka's defaults, the threshold 8)*. On an exact tie of a network split neither side holds a majority, and both stop their members while the split lasts, unless an operator takes members out of the log of the members, as a Raft group commits nothing on an even split (the owner, 2026-10-30, "Raft: neither side wins", against the side that holds the oldest machine running while the log of the members takes no join and no leave, as Akka's resolver keeps one side of a tie, at the cost of an operator's action and of a rule beside Raft's, and against an odd number of voting members, a member that only votes added where the count is even, at the cost of that member; the cost is an outage at every even split, which an odd number of members avoids). The operator's removal is no commit of the log of the members, which no side of an even split can make, and how it is made stands open (section 14).
- **Trust.** Members prove membership to each other with mutual TLS by default, each machine with a certificate from an authority of the cluster, and the traffic between them is encrypted (the owner, 2026-10-30, "Mutual TLS default", as Rust's ecosystem makes rustls the norm and ASP.NET Core's templates start with HTTPS on, against a shared secret as Erlang's cookie with TLS on request, at the cost of the exposure Erlang's own documentation warns of, and against no authentication on a network that must stay private, at the cost that one exposed port gives full control; the cost is a handshake for each connection, encryption of each message, certificates to issue and rotate, and the cipher primitives of section 2). A switch turns mutual TLS off, and then a member's port binds the loopback addresses alone, 127.0.0.1 and ::1, for tests and a cluster on one machine, while a cluster across machines needs TLS (the owner, 2026-10-30, "Loopback only", against a private range of addresses that the switch names, at the cost that an address is no proof of membership, and against a port open to anyone, as Erlang's without TLS, at the cost that whoever reaches the port reaches the cluster; the cost is no cluster in plain text across a trusted network). A member sends only through a reference it was given, an id of 128 bits that nobody can guess, or through a name registered as public, as a capability model grants (the owner, 2026-10-30, "References it holds", against anything, as an Erlang node calls any process, at the cost that one compromised member owns the cluster, and against public names alone, as gRPC serves named services, at the cost of a name in code for every actor called; the cost is that a reference has to reach a member before it sends, and the code that registers public names).
- **Delivery.** A `send` to a durable actor (section 13) is delivered one time or more, from an outbox that the sender logs on its disk (the owner, 2026-10-30, "Durable: at least once", against zero deliveries or one for every `send`, as Erlang delivers it, at the cost of a silent loss on a dropped link, and against one delivery or more for every `send`, with a buffer at the sender and duplicates removed by a message ID at the receiver, at the cost of memory at every sender and an ID for each message; the cost is writes to the sender's disk for those messages alone). A `send` to another actor on another machine is delivered one time or not at all, as Erlang delivers it *(assumed: what the answer leaves to the sends that do not go to a durable actor)*. Each `send` to a durable actor carries an id, and the actor's log records the ids for a window and drops a repeat, as Kafka's idempotent producer and Akka's delivery with ids do (the owner, 2026-10-30, "Drop by message id", against duplicates left to the program, at the cost that every durable handler has to be idempotent and a mistake shows only under failure; the cost is an id for each message and a window of ids in the log).
- **Inspection.** The runtime has an inspector of a running cluster: its actors on each machine, their inbox lengths and crash counts, and a snapshot of one actor's state with its `secret` fields stripped (section 13), behind the cluster's authentication (above) (the owner, 2026-10-30, "Read-only inspector", as .NET's diagnostic tools show a live process and BEAM's observer a node, against logs with chain IDs and crash traces alone, at the cost of a new build with more logging for a fault seen only in production, and against the inspector with record and replay switched on for one actor in production, at the cost of disk and CPU while it is on and of recordings that hold users' data; the cost is code in the runtime and one more port to secure, and nothing while nobody connects). It shows the live values of the instruments of section 12 too, as `dotnet-counters` reads a running process, and it has one write: it may set the level and the filter of the logs while the program runs, behind the same authentication (the owner, 2026-11-04, logging, tracing and metrics, Q10 (b) and Q13 (a), #274, comment 6643369246, against levels read at start alone and an inspector kept read-only, at the cost of a restart with a new level for a fault seen only in production, which loses the state the fault shows in, and of the new build with more logging named above where a ceiling removed the level (section 12), and against the settings file read again while the program runs, as ASP.NET's reloadable configuration, at the cost of a watch on the file while every other setting is read at start (section 12); the cost is an inspector that is no longer read-only, one more thing to secure, and the cached state of every call site rebuilt at each change).
- No hot code reload; it would cost runtime performance.
- **Upgrades:** code versions never mix inside one cluster. A new version forms a new cluster and traffic switches over. Clients outside the cluster are the exception (section 13). State moves only where an actor says so with `upgrade`:
  - No `upgrade` line: the actor starts fresh in the new cluster, the same as after a crash.
  - `upgrade keep field`: the field is carried over, matched by name and type. A new field gets its default, a removed field is dropped.
  - Block form for when the shape really changed.
  - A call parked in a durable actor (section 13) goes on in the new code: `kurz release` matches each wait point of the old code to one of the new code by method and position, and a wait point with no match is a build error that names it (the owner, 2026-10-30, "Release matches waits", against a parked call dropped and the actor started with its kept fields, at the cost that the trial of section 13's sample never ends, and against the old cluster serving its parked calls as long as one exists, at the cost of two clusters for up to the longest wait; the cost is compiler work of the kind `kurz release` does for the `pub` surface).
  - The log of a durable actor reaches the new cluster by copying: the new cluster's members join as copies of the log and catch up from a stream, and when they are current, the lead and the traffic move to them; the old cluster ends after the messages in flight (the owner, 2026-10-30, "Replicate, then switch", against a stop, a copy and a start, at the cost that the actor is unavailable while it is copied, and against a shared store with a lease, at the cost of a store outside the program under every durable actor; the cost is twice the log's storage during an upgrade).

```
actor UserStore {
    mut users = Map<int, User>()
    mut cache = Map<int, Page>()

    upgrade keep users                                          // cache starts empty
    upgrade (old) { users = old.users.Where(u => u.Active) }    // or transform by hand
}
```

```
every 5min on split run {
    RecountStock()
} merge (mine, theirs) => mine.Newer(theirs)
```

## 8. Syntax

- Variables: `x = 5` declares an immutable variable, `mut x = 5` a mutable one. The type may be written: `int x = 5`. An unused variable is a warning in a test build, the default one, and a compile error in a release build; either catches a typo that would otherwise declare a new variable (the owner, 2026-10-30, "Warn in test, error release", against the error in every build, as the record held it, at the cost of a broken build for every line commented out, and against a warning in every build, which a CI run can turn into an error, as Rust's lint is under `-D warnings`, at the cost that the check of typos depends on that flag; the cost is a diagnostic whose level the build sets). A parameter that its function never reads, and the variable of a `for` loop whose body never reads it, are no error (the owner, 2026-10-03, against making them errors like a variable, with the words that the compiler just optimizes it).
- No semicolons. A newline ends a statement. A `;` that ends, starts or follows a statement is the semicolon error, one for a run of them, and the statement after it parses on its own; a `;` anywhere else, inside parentheses, brackets or an interpolation, or where an operand, a name, a member, a parameter or an arm is expected, is the error for text no rule gives a meaning (the owner, 2026-10-10).
- No parentheses are needed around a condition, and braces are always required: `if x > 5 { ... }`. A condition in parentheses, `if (x > 5) {`, compiles all the same, since an expression in parentheses is an expression like any other; a `{` on the next line is the compile error for a missing block, because the line ends the statement and nothing continues it there (the owner, 2026-10-09, against continuing the statement onto the `{`, a further exception to the line rule, and against an error of its own for the parentheses, a special case in the parser for one spelling). The same error is raised wherever a block that a construct takes opens on the next line or is replaced by a statement, at the line where the block should have opened: the last line of the header of a `while` or a `for`, the line of the `match` or of the call an `else` follows, the line of the word `else` or `raw`, the line of the name or the word for the body of a `class`, `data`, `interface`, `enum` or `flags` or the braces of `with`, and the first line of the signature for the body of a function outside a type body or of a constructor; the list names the constructs the reference has cases or rules for, and the rule holds for every other block of this record, an `attempt` or `retry` block, an actor body and the block of `every ... run` among them, at the line where the words before the block end; a method signature inside a type body that ends its line is the bodiless form of an interface member, so its `{` on the next line is the error for text no rule gives a meaning (the owner, 2026-10-10).
- Signatures in C# order, type first: `User | NotFound Get(int id) => ...`.
- Everything is private by default: members are private to their type, top-level types and functions are private to their folder. `pub` exposes; `prot` exposes to inheriting types. The fields of a primary constructor are the exception: they can be read wherever their type is visible, as the positional members of a C# record can (the owner, 2026-10-02). Without that, every such field would carry `pub`. The cost: a field that has to stay private is declared in the body instead.
- A member marked `internal` is visible to the files of its folder, the unit a top-level type is already private to, and to nothing outside it, as C#'s `internal` is visible in its assembly and Rust's `pub(crate)` in its crate, so that the standard library lets one of its classes make another, `HttpRequest.Read` the request's `HttpBody`, without a program seeing the maker (the owner, 2026-11-02, the word, and 2026-11-03, the form; against Rust's `pub(folder)`, a form of `pub`, against a member without `pub` visible to its whole folder, as Go's lower-case names are visible to their package, at the cost that every private member of a class is seen by the rest of its folder, and against a `pub` maker that every program could call). *(assumed, not put to the owner: `internal` is a core word, as C# reserves it; `pub` and `internal` before one declaration are the error `syntax`, as C# refuses two access modifiers (CS0107); before a top-level type or function `internal` says what no modifier says, as C#'s `internal` is what a top-level type is without one.)*
- A folder is a namespace; there is no `namespace` line. Files in one folder see each other without imports. `use` brings in other folders and packages. A file names a folder of its project by its path from the folder of `project.kz`, `use a/util`, and the folder's last name qualifies what the file reaches through it, `util.Trim(s)` (section 13); two folders a file uses whose last names agree are a compile error at the second `use` line, which `as` fixes, `use b/util as butil` and `butil.Trim(s)`, as Go reads an import path and qualifies by the package's name, and as Rust refuses a second import of one name (its error E0252) (the owner, 2026-11-01, "Root path, last name", against the whole path as the qualifier, `a.util.Trim(s)`, as C#'s namespace written out, at the cost of long calls and of every call changed when a folder moves, and against a path relative to the folder of the file that uses it, `use ../a/util`, as C's `#include` and Node's `require`, at the cost that a moved file breaks its `use` lines; the cost is the rename by `as` of section 13, which two folders whose names agree need) *(assumed: the id `redeclared`, as Rust's E0252 reads the second import as a name defined twice; and, not put to the owner, that the names it compares are the qualifiers the `use` lines give, the name after `as`, or else a folder's last name, a package's line name or the last name of a longer path into a package, so that `use json` beside `use fastjson as json` is that error too, as E0252 compares the names two imports bind, and that a qualifier which a name at the top of the file's own folder has is `redeclared` at the `use` line, as Rust's E0255 refuses an import of a name an item of its module has, the `use` line being the one line of the file that meets the folder's name; and that a path that names no folder of the project and no line of `project.kz`, a path longer than a package's line name whose folder the package lacks, `use json/nosuch` where no folder `json` stands at the top (beside one, the answer of 2026-11-08 below), and a path that, after its first name, reaches or passes through a folder, of the project or of a package, that holds a `project.kz` of its own, which that package's line alone reaches and whose files the hash of the package around it leaves out (section 13), are `unknown-name` at the `use` line, as Rust's E0432 refuses an import that names nothing)* A `.` or `..` where a name of the path stands, `use ../util`, is `syntax`, as Rust's grammar of a `use` path holds names and the words `self`, `super` and `crate` alone, where Go writes an import path as a string and refuses a relative one in a module (the owner, 2026-11-04, "as built", against `unknown-name` at the `use` line, at the cost of a parser that reads `.` and `..` as names of a path; the cost is that the error names the `.` found and not the path). The reading reads a project's files: the `use sys` and `use std` of the runtime's `common/` and `std/` stand as section 2 makes them, and in a program's file `use sys` and `use std` are paths like any other, which a folder at the top of the project or a line of `project.kz` of that name answers, and which are an unknown name where the project has neither (the owner, 2026-11-03, "the runtime's names only", as Rust keeps `std::sys` private to its standard library and section 12 lets every file see the types of `std/` with no `use`, against `std` for every program, as Rust's `std` stands in every crate's extern prelude, at the cost that the `pub` functions at the top of `std/` are a surface every program reaches and the name is taken from every project, and against `sys` too for every program, at the cost that the runtime's functions of each target are such a surface, where Rust keeps `sys` private; the cost is that no program reaches a function at the top of `std/` by name). A `use` line whose name is both a folder at the top of the project and a line of `project.kz`, `use json` beside a folder `json`, is the compile error `ambiguous-name` at that line, as C#'s CS0104 is given for a name that two namespaces give: nothing is picked without a word, and the folder is renamed or the line dropped (the owner, 2026-11-02, against the project's folder first, as Rust 2018 reads a local module before an external crate of that name ("a path beginning with that name will be taken to refer to the local module or item", the edition guide, "Extern crate paths", whose "`use` paths" says that paths in `use` declarations and in other code work the same way; what rustc gives for such a name in a `use` declaration was not checked), at the cost that the package is reached by no spelling Kurz has, where Rust writes `::json`, and against the package first; the cost is a folder renamed or a line dropped where their names agree). The error stands in every file of the project, those of the folder `json` included, and with `as`, `use json as j` naming two things as `use json` does, as C#'s CS0104 is given for an alias whose target is ambiguous (the owner, 2026-11-02, against reading `use json` inside that folder as the package, and against `as` picking the package) *(assumed, not put to the owner, as these two sentences read a name that both give: a longer path whose first name is both, `use json/schema`, is that error at its `use` line too; and a folder at the top that holds a `project.kz` of its own is no folder of the project (section 13, "Where a package sits"), so that `use json` beside such a folder names the line)*. A longer path whose first name is both a folder at the top and a line of `project.kz`, and whose rest neither holds, `use json/nosuch`, is `ambiguous-name` at its `use` line too, not `unknown-name`: the path's first name is read before the rest, as the answer of 2026-11-02 above reads `use json` (the owner, 2026-11-08, #381, comment 6721436168, "ambiguous-name", against `unknown-name` first, which would leave the clash of the two names unreported until the path names something), at the cost that a path neither of the two holds sends its writer to rename the folder or drop the line, the path's own `unknown-name` following once the clash is gone, a cost the question did not name. A path longer than a package's line name reaches that package's folder: with a line `json` of `project.kz` and no folder `json` at the top of the project, `use json/schema` reaches the folder `schema` of that package, as a project's own `use a/util` reaches its folder `a/util` (the owner, 2026-11-04, "with only a `json` dependency line, `use json/schema` reaches that package's subfolder", against `unknown-name`, a package's line reaching its top folder alone, at the cost that a package holds all its code at its top; the cost is that a package's inner folders become paths its users reach, so that moving one breaks their `use` lines, both costs the owner's of 2026-11-05). *(assumed, with the build: a space beside a `/` of a path reads as one between any two tokens, `use a / util` being `use a/util`, as Rust reads `a :: b`, and a line break ends the path, so that `use a/` is `syntax`)*
- The project file is written in Kurz itself (`project.kz`), not in a separate format. It holds one `deploy` block per deployment with that deployment's switches: the inbox mode (section 13) and, by the same idea, distribution on or off and the target platform. *(assumed)*
- String interpolation is always on: `"hello {name}"`, in every literal but a raw one (below).
- A string over several lines is written as a raw string literal is in C# 11: it opens with `"""` at the end of a line and closes with `"""` on a line of its own. The text starts on the line after the opening and ends before the closing line, and the indentation of the closing line is removed from every line; a line that is indented less is a compile error, as there (the owner, 2026-10-02). A `"` inside the block is an ordinary character, as there. Unlike there, `{expression}` and `\` keep the meaning they have in every other literal, so a brace of JSON or CSS is written `\{` (the owner, 2026-10-02, against a block without interpolation, which was the form offered). `"""` opens a block only at the end of a line: `"""abc"""` on one line, text after an opening `"""` and text before a closing one are compile errors, and a line of the block that holds only whitespace is exempt from the indentation rule and is an empty line of the text, as in C# 11 (the owner, 2026-10-09, against a one-line form that holds `abc` with a `"` as an ordinary character, as C# 11 has it, and against an id of its own for the malformed shapes; the escape gives a `"` without the one-line form). Only characters other than whitespace count as text beside a `"""`, as C# 11 has it, so trailing spaces after the opening and the indentation before the closing are no error; and code may follow the closing `"""` on its line, `""")` closing a call, as C# 11 allows, since "on a line of its own" is about what stands before it (the owner, 2026-10-10, confirming the reading proposed after the review of round 13). There is no block that opens with four or more quotes, which C# 11 allows: `""""` at the end of a line is a compile error (the owner, 2026-10-10). A lone carriage return, one that no line feed follows, is an ordinary character inside a literal, except at the end of a line of the block, where every trailing one is dropped with the line's end, and whitespace outside a literal, so a file whose lines end in a carriage return alone is one line, which does not compile as its writer meant; the cost is nothing, since no current editor writes those line ends (the owner, 2026-10-10).
- A raw literal, `r"\d{2,4}"`, holds its text as it is written, with no escape and no interpolation, as Rust's raw string literal does: a `\` and a `{` are ordinary characters in it, so a pattern or a JSON text reads as it does in the documentation of the language it comes from. `r#"say "hi""#` holds a `"`, as Rust's `#` form does, and a raw block stands beside the block above, with no escape and no interpolation in its text (the owner, 2026-11-01, "Rust's raw r\"...\"", asked with a pattern written as `"\\d\{2,4}"` under the escapes, against C#'s verbatim literal, `@"\d{2,4}"` with `""` for a quote, at the same cost in C#'s spelling, against a pattern literal of its own, `/\d{2,4}/`, as JavaScript's, at the cost of a third kind of literal and a `/` read as division beside it, and against the escapes as they are, at the cost of every class and every brace doubled in every pattern and every JSON text; the cost is a second kind of literal in the lexer, and a reader must know which form keeps escapes). This revisits the answer of 2026-10-02 (above) for the raw forms alone: every literal that is not raw keeps its escapes and its interpolation. *(assumed, each proposed with this record and not put to the owner: that the raw block opens with `r"""` at the end of a line and takes every rule of the block above, its line ends, its indentation and its shapes; that `r#"` opens with one to 255 `#` and closes at a `"` followed by as many, as Rust's lexer counts them; that a raw literal ends on the line it starts on, as an ordinary literal does, where Rust's runs over lines, since the raw block holds several lines; that a raw block has no `#` form, as the block has no form of four quotes; that an `r` directly before `"` or before `#` and a `"` starts a raw literal wherever a name could start, where a name `r` followed by a string was text no rule gives a meaning; that a raw literal that does not end on its line is the error an ordinary one is, and a raw block of a wrong shape the error a block of that shape is; and that a raw literal stands wherever a literal does, an interpolation's hole and an `asm` template among them, where its `{name}` names an operand as in any template)*.
- Primary constructors, C# lambdas, C# generics.
- Top-level statements instead of `Main`.
- A statement continues on the next line while a `(` or a `[` is open, when its line ends in a binary operator, a comma or `=>`, and when the next line starts with `.`. Nothing else continues it. There is no `;`: not at the end of a line and not between two statements. (the owner, 2026-10-02) The `=` of an assignment counts as a binary operator here. *(assumed)* In detail, each a reading of one of the three exceptions (the owner, 2026-10-10): a line that starts with `?.` continues the statement as one that starts with `.` does, and empty lines and comment lines between the statement and that line do not end it; a line break inside the braces of an `enum`, `flags` or `with` body and inside the `< >` of type arguments or type parameters does not end the statement, as one inside parentheses does not; a line break after the `:` of a base list continues the declaration; a line that ends in the `|` of a type or in `..` or `..<` continues on the next; and a trailing comma is accepted in an `enum` or `flags` body and between the brackets of a list (section 4), and refused in the braces of `with`, where it is the error for text no rule gives a meaning (section 8). A line that starts with `.` directly followed by a digit starts a statement with a fraction literal (above) and continues nothing (the owner, 2026-10-11, confirming the reading proposed after the review of round 14).
- `name = expression` assigns when a variable of that name is visible and declares one when none is, so a variable cannot hide another one. A variable counts as used when it is read at least once; being assigned again does not count. A `mut` variable that nothing changes is a warning, not an error. (the owner, 2026-10-02)
- A written type always declares; when the name is already visible that is a compile error. A variable is visible from its declaration to the end of its block, and every declaration has a value. *(assumed)*
- `a..b` is a range that includes both ends, `a..<b` leaves the end out. A loop over numbers is `for i in 0..<n`; the C form with three parts does not exist. (the owner, 2026-10-02) A range never counts down, and a range whose end lies below its start is an error, not an empty range: a compile error when both ends are constant expressions, an exception when the program runs otherwise (the owner, 2026-10-02, against the proposal that such a range holds no number). `a..<a` holds no number and is valid. The cost: `for i in 1..n` throws when `n` is 0, so a loop that may run zero times is written with `..<`. The range and its loop variable have the common type of the two ends, found as `+` finds it: `0..<n` with a `long` `n` is a range of `long`, and integer ends for which `+` raises the error for mixing signed with unsigned are that error (the owner, 2026-10-09, against a range that is always `int`, under which a loop over a `long` range is written by hand; the cost is that the loop variable's type follows the end, which a reader finds at the declaration of `n`). An end whose type is no integer type, `0..<1.5` or `0..2.0` whatever its value, is the error for a value of one type where another is required (the owner, 2026-10-10, confirming the reading proposed after the review of round 13).
- `else` and `else if` follow the closing brace on its line; a condition is a `bool`; `while condition { }`, `for name in collection { }`, `break` and `continue` mean what they mean in C#. *(assumed)*
- A function body is an expression after `=>` or a block with `return`; a function without a result is declared `void`; a function or a type can be used above its declaration. *(assumed)* `void` is no type of a value: a parameter a function declares, a field or a variable of type `void` is refused, as C# refuses each (CS1536, CS0670, CS1547), while the success case of a union and the result of a function type may be `void` (above) (the owner, 2026-11-04, comment 6643376941 on issue 156, answering its comment 6619221311, against a type with one value, as Rust's `()`, at the cost of a second meaning of `void` beside a function's declaration, a reading of the type argument against T17 and the emitter's work for a value of no size, and against an id of its own, such as `void-value`, at the cost of one more id for the same refusal; no cost beyond the rule). A parameter of a function type, `(void) => int`, is read as it is (the same answer, against refusing it as C# refuses it in a delegate, CS1536, at the cost that a program that writes one is refused; the cost is a function value whose parameter can hold no value).
- Functions may share a name when their parameters differ, a parameter or a field may have a default value (`int Count = 1`), and an argument may be passed by name (`Item(ProductId: 7)`). The owner chose overloads on 2026-10-02 against the proposal to leave them out. When a call fits several functions, the one whose parameters have exactly the types of the arguments, with no default value used, wins; any other call that fits more than one is a compile error (the owner, 2026-10-02). The cost of that rule: where two functions fit through widening, the call needs a conversion such as `long(x)`. For this rule a literal argument has the type it has on its own, `int` for `4`, so `Show(4)` picks `Show(int)` over `Show(long)`, as in C# (the owner, 2026-10-02). A call of a name that has more than one function and fits none of them is the compile error `argument-mismatch`, at the call, with a message that names each function and why it does not fit (the owner, 2026-10-21, against the error of the first function, in the order of declaration, that the arguments bind to, under which the error changes when two declarations swap places; the cost is a longer message, and an id that no longer names the argument's own fault, such as a narrowing conversion). *(assumed: that the line is the first line of the call, as an error of the whole construct reports it (below); the answer said at the call)* A method or a property that the place of the call does not see (above) is no candidate of the call where the place sees one of its name: a call from a class that fits only a method or a property of a base the class does not see gets the error of the methods of that name the place sees, a base's it sees among them, and the message of `argument-mismatch` above names those alone, as C# leaves an inaccessible member out of overload resolution (CS7036, CS1501) (the owner, 2026-11-06, #39, comment 6680927192, "(A)", against keeping such a member a candidate and refusing the call with the error for a name that is not visible, as Rust reports a private method its lookup found (E0624), at the cost of an error about a member the class cannot see; the cost is a filter of the candidates by what the class sees, and an error that does not name the base's method). Where the place sees no method of the name, the call is the error for a name that is not visible whatever its arguments, as C#'s CS0122 and Rust's E0624 report a hidden method before its arguments (the owner, 2026-11-06, #39, comment 6693534129, "(A)", against that error only where the call fits a member the place does not see, under which a call that fits none got the error of a call that fits none) *(assumed: the cost, an error that does not say what the arguments lack while the method is hidden, which the answer did not name; that a base's method the place sees stays among the methods whose error the call gets, where the answer named the class's own method; that the candidates are counted after the filter, so that a call whose place sees one method of the name gets that method's own error, as a call of a name with one function does; that the arguments of a call whose place sees no method of the name are checked for their own errors; and that the error names the nearest of those methods, the first along the chain of the class whose method is called, which the answer did not say)*. *(assumed: a reading of the answer of comment 6680927192, which named a call from the class: a call outside every class, through an instance, picks among the methods its place sees too)* The cost of overloads as such: a name no longer stands for one function, for the reader and for `mock` (section 11), and the name of a parameter becomes something its callers depend on. Arguments are evaluated from left to right, as in C# *(assumed: proposed on 2026-10-09 and not objected to)*, in the order written at the call, named arguments included (the owner, 2026-10-10). A parameter's default value is a constant expression, as C# requires of it: a literal, `null`, a value of an `enum` or `flags`, a `data` value without fields, or an expression of literals that section 4 folds (the owner, 2026-10-11, confirming the reading proposed after the review of round 14), and a `data` value made by its name whose every argument is such a constant, `HttpRate(240, 5s)`, which goes beyond C#, where `new S()` is a default only for a value type `S` and only without arguments (CS1736), while `HttpRate(n, 1s)` with a variable `n` stays no constant (the owner, 2026-11-03, against any expression as a default, evaluated at each call that leaves it out as Kotlin evaluates one, at the cost of a rule for its side effects and its order, and against `HttpLimits` (section 12) as a class whose fields have defaults, which would reverse its choice of 2026-10-31, "HttpLimits data") *(assumed: the reading that such a value, being a constant, may itself be an argument of another, `Pair(Rate(1, 1s), Rate(2, 2s))`, that a field it leaves out takes its own default (D11), which this rule holds to a constant where the field is declared, and that an instance of a class is no such value; and the cost, that such a value is made at each call that leaves the argument out, as the construction it is written as; not put to the owner)*; one that is not is the compile error `default-not-constant`, at the parameter (the owner, 2026-10-10, against the general type error and the id for text no rule gives a meaning; the spelling of the id and its line are *(assumed: proposed on 2026-10-10, after the owner's choice)*). The default of a field of a class body may be any expression (the owner, 2026-10-10, against constants alone, under which a field of a collection type could have no default): it may read the parameters of the primary constructor, the fields declared above it and functions outside the class, and is evaluated in declaration order before the body of a constructor runs, as C# evaluates an initializer, which refuses an instance member there; a field declared below it, a method of its instance or `this` is the error for a name that is not visible, while a `static` method of the class is a name there, as C# refuses an instance member in an initializer and no `static` one (the owner, 2026-11-02, against every method of the class refused there); the cost is that such a default runs at every construction, which a constant one does not, a `data` value of constants apart (above) (the owner, 2026-10-11, confirming the reading proposed after the review of round 14). The default of a parameter of a method, `static` or not, is a constant as a function's is, and is read with the members of its class in sight, as C# reads it: a field, a `static` field or a method of the class named there is no constant, so it is the error for a default that is not one, as C# gives CS1736 for a `static readonly` field (the owner, 2026-11-04, comment 6643376941 on issue 156, answering its comment 6619751130, against reading it as a function's default, with no member in sight, where such a name is the error for a name that is not visible, at the cost that a developer who comes from C# reads that error as a defect of the compiler while the class has the field; the cost is a second way of reading a default in the checker, in the scope of the class) *(assumed: `this` in the default of an instance method is no constant either, and `this` or a member of an instance, a field or a method, named in the default of a `static` method is the error a `static` member gives for it in its body, as C# refuses it there too, in place of the error for a default that is not one: a narrowing of the answer above for a member of an instance in a `static` method, which the answer does not name)*. A call of a `virtual` method or of its override takes the default of the method its receiver's static type names, and runs the body the object's type gives, as C# does: with `virtual F(int x = 1)` in `A` and `override F(int x = 2)` in `B`, `A a = B(); a.F()` passes 1 to `B`'s body and `B().F()` passes 2, and an override without a default has none of its own, so `B().F()` lacks the argument there (the owner, 2026-11-05, comment 6659240390 on issue 156, answering its comment 6659145995, against Kotlin's rule, under which an override declares no default and takes the base's, at the cost of a refusal of a default on an override and a departure from C#, and against a default on a `virtual` method or an override left unread until an answer, at the cost that a program that wants one waits for the answer; the cost is that one object's call passes different values by the type of the variable it is read through, which ReSharper's inspection of a mismatched optional parameter reports). A default of a field of a class body that builds its own class at every construction it runs in, itself or through the default of a class it builds, runs again at each construction it makes, so that the run recurses until it ends in `stack-overflow` (section 6), as C# recurses on an initializer that constructs its own class, while a guarded one, which builds it on some paths alone, runs the constructions it makes as written and ends where they end (the owner, 2026-11-02, against a compile error with an id of its own for every default that builds its own class, which would narrow "any expression" and refuse a guarded default too, and against one for a default that builds it on every path, at the cost of a walk in the checker; the cost is that a default which recurses on every path is found when it runs).

A file that is not valid UTF-8, an encoded surrogate included, is one compile error, `invalid-source`, at the line of the first bad byte; a byte-order mark at the start of the file is skipped, because some Windows editors and tools write one (the owner, 2026-10-09, against refusing the mark too, under which a file saved with the mark does not compile; the cost is one accepted leading code point that is not part of the text). No conformance case shows the error: the lint and every gate read a corpus file as UTF-8, so a case that is not would be refused by the tools as they stand, and the reference names the id in its rule and not in its table of the ids cases expect. The two-byte line break that Windows editors write is read as one line break wherever it stands in a source file, inside a `"""` block too, so the same program compiles and prints the same text whether its lines end in a line feed or in the two-byte break (the owner, 2026-10-10, against reading the two bytes as written, under which the text of a block depends on the editor; the cost is that no string literal can hold the two-byte line break as written: a carriage return directly before a line feed is written through its escape, where a carriage return that no line feed follows stands as written). No conformance case can show it either: the repository stores every file with line feeds alone, and checks them out so on every platform (`.gitattributes`, `* text=auto eol=lf`). A carriage return that no line feed follows is read as the rule on strings over several lines says, above.
- `//` starts a comment that runs to the end of its line. In a string literal that is not raw (above) `\n`, `\t`, `\"` and `\\` mean what they mean in C#, and `\{` is a brace that starts no interpolation; the other escapes of C# 12 (`\'`, `\0`, `\a`, `\b`, `\f`, `\r`, `\v`, `\u` with four hex digits, `\U` with eight and `\x` with one to four) mean what they mean there, and a backslash before any other character, or before a `u`, `U` or `x` without the digits it takes, is a compile error, as there (the owner, 2026-10-03, against the five alone; the version, under which the `\e` of C# 13 is such an error, is *(assumed)*). A `\u`, `\U` or `\x` whose digits name a surrogate, U+D800 to U+DFFF, or a value beyond U+10FFFF is that error too, since a string holds code points and not UTF-16 units (the owner, 2026-10-10); a pair of such escapes that C# would join, `\uD83D\uDE00`, is the error at the first, and `\U0001F600` writes the code point (the owner, 2026-10-11, confirming the reading proposed after the review of round 14). `true` and `false` are the values of `bool`. A name starts with a letter or `_` and goes on with letters, digits and `_`; upper and lower case differ. A letter is one of ASCII's: a name with any other character, an umlaut included, is a compile error, and C#'s `@` names do not exist (the owner, 2026-10-09, against any Unicode letter as C# allows, under which two names can look the same, and against `@keyword` names, a second spelling C# has for interop; the cost is that a C# program with an umlaut in a name is edited). *(assumed: the comment, the five escapes, `true` and `false`, and the rest of the form of a name)*

Such an error that only the type checker can see, a `match` on a set of flags or a call with a `void` success used as a value, is reported at the line of the construct (the owner, 2026-10-10). ## 9. Keywords that transform code

- Core words live in the compiler: `actor`, `data`, `match`, `mut`, `spawn`, `weak`, `pub` and the like.
- Chore keywords are written in Kurz, with the same mechanism users get, and ship in the standard library.
- Chores that should become keywords:
  - HTTP endpoints and routing
  - retry, timeout, circuit breaker around a call
  - caching
  - mapping between types
  - validation
  - database queries
  - scheduled jobs
  - state machines
  - dependency wiring
  - the span of a trace around a block, `span` (section 12), while a log call is a call of the standard library and no keyword (the owner, 2026-11-04, logging, tracing and metrics, Q1 (a) and Q3 (c), #274, comment 6643369246)

### User-defined keywords

Users can define full block keywords. The rules that keep editor tooling easy:

1. **Free shape, declared as a pattern.** The head is built from slots: fixed words, expressions, types, names, blocks, declarations, with optional and repeated parts. The pattern is data the editor reads without running code. A keyword starts with its own word, and two keywords used in one file may not overlap.
2. **The inside is plain Kurz.** A keyword never adds new syntax inside its slots.
3. **Declared and imported.** A file names the keywords it uses.
4. **The output is plain Kurz and viewable.** Errors point at the developer's source, not at the expansion.
5. **Sealed at compile time.** Keyword code cannot read files, network or clock.
6. **No capture.** A keyword only touches what is passed to it. Names it introduces inside its body are declared in its pattern.
7. **Read-only type information.** A keyword may inspect the fields and methods of types it is given.
8. **No redefining** built-in keywords or each other.

```
keyword every <duration interval> [per <scope where>] <block body>
keyword route <verb> <string path> <method handler>
keyword retry <int times> <block body> [else <block fallback>]
```

- A package that defines keywords needs a grant of its own in `project.kz`, as one that touches files or the network does (section 13), so that a team sees and chooses the forms it admits (the owner, 2026-10-30, "Grant for keywords", against the eight rules alone, at the cost that each package adds its own form for a chore and two code bases read differently, and against a rule of the design that a new core form names the form it supersedes and the older one draws a warning, at the cost of a judgment in every design round; the cost is one more grant). The grant goes to the package that defines keywords alone, written `allow keywords "pkg"` beside `allow raw`, and a package that uses its keywords needs nothing (the owner, 2026-10-30, "Definer, `allow keywords`", against a grant for each package that uses them, at the cost of a line for each such package and of forms that read differently from package to package; the cost is that a project cannot admit a keyword for one part of it alone) *(assumed: that `"pkg"` stands for the name of the package that defines the keywords)*.

## 10. Scheduled jobs

- Position gives the default scope; `per` overrides it.
- Defaults: ticks follow the clock, a tick is skipped if the previous run is still going, ticks missed during downtime are dropped. A job never runs in parallel with itself.
- `at 03:00 daily` names an hour in UTC unless the code writes a zone (section 12, decided there).

```
every 5min { CleanupSessions() }          // top level: once in the cluster
every 5min per node { FlushMetrics() }    // on each machine

actor Session {
    every 30s { Ping() }                  // inside an actor: belongs to each instance
}

every 30s after done { }                  // 30s after the last run finished
every 30s overlap queue { }               // queue a tick instead of skipping it
every 30s catchup { }                     // run ticks missed during downtime
at 03:00 daily { }                        // calendar schedule
```

## 11. Dependency injection and tests

- There is no container. A singleton is an actor declared `per cluster` or `per node` and addressed by its type name (section 13). For actors spawned by hand, wiring is constructor parameters.
- A service with no state is plain functions, or a class with constructor parameters, run on its caller's actor; `per cluster` and `per node` are for state that must be single; and state that many actors read and few change is a snapshot that one actor publishes and any actor on the machine that holds it reads without a message, as an `Arc` that its owner swaps gives it in Rust and an ETS table in Elixir (the owner, 2026-10-30, "Functions + snapshots", against the record as it stood, under which every service is one actor and one queue for all its callers, the shape Elixir's documentation calls an anti-pattern, and against an actor that runs its methods that change no state on many cores at a time, at the cost of section 6's one message at a time and of a marking of reads and writes; the cost is a rule of usage, a `mock` that reaches such a class as it reaches an actor, and for a snapshot one atomic load for each read, a copy for each publish and a new kind of shared value). *(assumed: the words "on the machine that holds it", as an `Arc` and an ETS table are local to one process and one node)*; how an actor on another machine reads it is open (section 14).
- Tests swap implementations with `mock`. The swap happens at compile time, inside the `test` block that writes it, and reaches only what that test runs: a program's own run swaps nothing, in the test build, which the command builds unless `--release` is given (section 2, decided there), as in the release one, since `build`, `run` and `exec` run no `test` block; the `test` blocks of a program run under `kurz test file.kz`, as `dotnet test` runs a project's tests (checked 2026-10-20: the documentation of `dotnet test`), and the swap is in effect in the build that command makes, inside the test that writes it, and nowhere else; each test under `kurz test` gets instances of its own of the singletons it reaches, of those the program declares (above, and section 13, decided there), each spawned for that test at the test's first message to it, in the build its swaps make, so a test reaches the instances spawned for it and no other test's, and a singleton no test reaches is not spawned, and the instances a program's own run would spawn do not run under a test; the name of the test build of section 2 (decided there) names the overflow checks of section 4 and not the running of tests *(assumed: the command `kurz test` and its name, proposed with this record and not put to the owner)*; so no interface has to exist just for faking; the cost is that the code a test reaches is compiled one time per distinct set of swaps, a compile-time and binary-size cost that grows with the tests that mock different things, and one spawn of each singleton per test that reaches it *(assumed: that the swap reaches the test alone, the singletons a test reaches spawned one per test, at its first message, and its cost, the spawn per test among it, proposed with this record and not put to the owner)*.

```
test "rename fails for unknown user" {
    mock UserStore with FakeStore
    ...
}
```

- The runtime owns clock and scheduler, so a test can fast-forward virtual time. Timers, jobs and the timeouts whose wait the runtime owns all fire, and the test takes milliseconds; a blocking read is the exception (below). In a test `instant.Now` (section 12) and `timestamp.Now` read the runtime's clock, which `advance` moves, and no clock is passed in (the owner, 2026-11-04, the monotonic clock, Q7 (a), #110, comment 6643368937, against a clock value passed to every function that reads the time, as .NET's `TimeProvider` and its `FakeTimeProvider`, at the cost of a parameter on every path that reads the time, which "Deadline on chain ID" chose against (section 6), and against a `mock` of a clock that the standard library reads through an interface, at the cost of a fake that each test writes; the cost is that a test build's runtime holds the offset that `advance` adds to each read, while a release build reads the clock directly, and that a blocking read waits in the kernel, in real time, which `advance` does not shorten, so that a test of a bound on a blocking server sets small limits, since `HttpLimits` is data (section 12), and waits them out, and `advance` reaches a bound only where the runtime owns the wait, which on an actor's socket hangs on how that socket's bound is held, an item of section 14) *(assumed: the defaults of the round, not objected to: the real clock keeps running in a test and `advance` adds to it, so that a real wait shows in the time that passed)*.

```

    server = spawn TcpServer
    advance 60days
```

## 12. Standard library

Everything is self-written. Tiers:

- **Core** (runs on microcontrollers): numbers, strings, collections, math, time.
- **Runtime:** actors, supervisors, scheduler, timers, clustering, serialization, `Stream<T>`.
- **System:** files, processes, environment, TCP/UDP, DNS.
- **Backend:** HTTP server and client, TLS, `Sealed<T>`, logging, the chore keywords.
- **Data:** database driver and the query keyword. MySQL first; the wire driver is built last.
- **Tooling:** test runner, formatter, editor language server. Package manager later.
- **Not in the box:** graphics, audio, windowing. These are packages over the C-ABI.

Database:

- Queries compile to SQL at build time, so SQL mistakes are compile errors and nothing is translated at run time.
- LINQ-style chains for the common case, checked raw SQL for complex queries. Interpolated values become parameters.
- A chain is lazy, and its read consumes it: it runs where it is read, and a second read of the same chain is a compile error, as a Rust iterator moved into a `for` loop cannot be used again, so that a program that reads twice writes `ToList()` (the owner, 2026-10-30, "Consumed by its read", against a chain that runs where it is assigned and gives a `List<T>`, at the cost of the whole result in memory and no streaming of a large one, and against a chain that runs again at each read, as C#'s `IEnumerable<T>`, at the cost of C#'s second query without a word; the cost is a check of single use in the compiler) *(assumed: that a `Stream<T>` (section 13) is consumed by its read in the same way, the question having named it beside the chain)*.
- Both schema directions are supported. Code first: the database is generated from `data` types. Database first: a tool command (`kurz db pull`, in the manner of `dotnet ef`) connects through the wire driver package and writes the schema into the repository as generated Kurz. Builds read only that file, so compilation stays sealed (section 9, rule 5).
- Failures: an unreachable database is an exception (supervisor and `retry` deal with it). A constraint violation or a missing row is a union case.

Migrations, code first:

- A migration is generated by diff, kept in the repository and editable: `kurz db migrate "add size"`, in the manner of `dotnet ef migrations add`. Three differences from EF:
  - A rename is stated in code (`string FullName was Name`) and never guessed as drop plus add.
  - There is no model snapshot file. The compiler replays the migrations to know the schema before, so nothing conflicts on merge.
  - SQL inside a migration is checked against the schema as of that step.
- The new cluster applies pending migrations itself, once (one machine, a cluster-wide lock), before traffic switches. A tool command (`kurz db update`) exists for pipelines that want the step explicit.
- Old and new version share the database during the switch, so the compiler splits every migration in two. Steps that are safe for the old code (a new table, a new column with a default, a new index) run before the switch. Steps that break the old code (drop, tighten) run after the old cluster is gone.
  - The compiler knows every column the old release touches, because all queries are compiled and `kurz release` snapshots them.
  - A step that cannot be made safe is a build error that names the old query it breaks.
  - A renamed column keeps its old physical name until the second phase.
  - There are no down scripts. Before the second phase nothing is destroyed, so rolling back is switching traffic back.

Database first: migrations belong to whoever owns the database. After a change, `kurz db pull`, and the compiler flags every query that no longer fits.

```
users = db.Users.Where(u => u.Age > 18).OrderBy(u => u.Name).Take(10)
users = sql "SELECT * FROM users WHERE age > {minAge}"
```

Hints:

- `Hint.BlackBox(x)` gives back its argument and tells the optimiser nothing of it, Rust's `std::hint::black_box` in Kurz's casing, as `Command.New` is Rust's `Command::new`. It asks the optimiser, as best effort (below), to know no constant of the value after the call and to keep the work that made it, so that a benchmark keeps the work it measures (the owner, 2026-11-03, "`Hint.BlackBox(x)`", against `Hint.Opaque(x)`, at the cost of a name no reader knows from elsewhere, and against a bare `BlackBox(x)`, at the cost of a name taken in every program and no home for a second hint). `Hint` is a name every file sees, so a file's own `Hint` is `redeclared`, and it is the home of any later hint, such as Rust's `spin_loop`. C# has no such hint: .NET code writes a method of its own marked `[MethodImpl(MethodImplOptions.NoInlining)]` that returns its argument, at the cost of a real call, and `GC.KeepAlive(obj)` keeps an object alive and hides no value.
- It takes a value of any type, as Rust's does, `T Hint.BlackBox<T>(T value)` with `T` inferred from the argument, numbers, `bool`, `char`, strings, lists, maps, class instances and `data` values among them, a string or a list by its handle (the owner, 2026-11-03, "Any value, as Rust's", against numbers, `bool` and `char` alone, at the cost that a benchmark cannot hide the string it searches or the list it sorts). An argument with no type of its own is refused as for any generic function: `Hint.BlackBox([])` is `cannot-infer` (M11, T27), as an untyped lambda is (T27) *(assumed: `Hint.BlackBox(null)` is `type-mismatch`, as N6 assumes of a `null` with no nullable type, and a call with another count of arguments than one is `argument-mismatch`, the id D11 proposes; type arguments are refused with `syntax` (E4), as `string.Join` refuses them, and a member of `Hint` other than `BlackBox` is `unknown-name`, as a function `Sha256` lacks is)*.
- Every program may call it, and it needs no `raw`, as Rust's needs no `unsafe`: it is the identity. It is best effort, in Rust's words: a program's correctness rests on nothing but its being the identity, and it promises nothing of constant time or of security, since LLVM promises nothing more of an empty `asm`. It is lowered as rustc lowers Rust's: the value goes to a slot, an empty `asm sideeffect` takes the slot's address with a memory clobber, and the value is read back (the owner, 2026-11-03, "The defaults of the round stand"). The memory clobber costs the code around the call: LLVM takes the call as one that may read and write any memory a pointer reaches, so it keeps every store to such memory before the call and reads such memory again after it, while a value in a register, or in a local whose address no code takes, stays. Measured on MD5 with the hint at each of its 64 step constants, 16 MiB three times, best of 15: 51.78 ms fall to 42.60 ms, 0.95× of .NET's 44.62 ms, and the value held in a register took 42.60 ms with a memory clobber and 42.58 ms without one, each at 4034 instructions in the block's function against the slot's 4144: on MD5 the 110 instructions more come from the slot, not from the clobber.

## 13. Further features

Agreed in a later brainstorm round. Each one is compiled into a program only when the program uses it.

### Actors addressed by key or by name

`per` on an actor says how many of it exist and where:

```
actor Cache per node { }            // one per machine:    Cache.Get(key)
actor Billing per cluster { }       // one in the cluster: Billing.Charge(order)
actor Session per int userId { }    // one per key:        Session[42].Add(item)
actor Cart per caller { }           // one per signed-in client (see "Clients and devices")
actor Circuit per connection { }    // one per client connection
actor Worker { }                    // spawned by hand, the reference is passed around
```

No spawn, no lookup, no registry. The runtime finds a keyed actor or creates it on some machine, places each key, puts idle actors to sleep and rebalances when machines join. For the developer this is horizontal scaling with zero code; the cost is compiler and runtime work. It needs a cluster-wide directory, and during a network split the three-step rule of section 7 applies per key.

- A `per cluster` or `per node` actor is the singleton: no registration and no wiring, and `mock` works on it unchanged. The dependency is no longer visible in a constructor; the compiler can list who uses what.
- A keyed actor that is not `durable` is dropped after an idle time: 10 minutes by default, overridable (`idle 10min` as a sketch). Its state is gone and the next call starts it fresh.

### Durable actors

```
durable actor Subscription per int userId {
    mut plan = Plan.Free
    pub void Trial() {
        plan = Plan.Pro
        wait 30days
        plan = Plan.Free
    }
}
```

Every change reaches an actor as a message, so logging messages to disk makes its state survive crashes and restarts. A log on the local disk does not survive the loss of the machine, which the first version of this section claimed. `durable` therefore has three modes:

- Local disk only: one disk write per message; the state is lost with the machine.
- A copy on N machines before a message counts as stored (`durable 2`): survives the loss of a machine and costs a network round trip per message.
- A copy sent in the background: fast, and the last moments are lost when the machine dies.

The default is two copies when distribution is on and local disk on a single machine. The spelling of the first and third mode is not fixed. Enabled only where the `durable` keyword is used. Kurz gets its own storage engine for this, written in Kurz.

During a network split (section 7), a message counts as stored only where a majority of the actor's copies took it on the side that holds the cluster's majority *(assumed: "a majority of the actor's copies", of the default two copies both; whether an actor of three copies or more needs all of them, as the mode above says, or a majority, as the comparison below reads Raft and Kafka, stands open, section 14)*, and the side without it refuses a durable `send` with an error while the split lasts, its members stopping after the detector's window (below), as Raft commits an entry and as Kafka's `min.insync.replicas` refuses a write (the owner, 2026-10-30, "Majority side only", against both sides taking messages and merging them after the split, as Dynamo and Riak, at the cost of histories in conflict or lost messages; the cost is that the side without the majority takes no durable message during a split). With the default of two copies (above) a message needs both, so a split that puts the two copies on two sides refuses the durable `send`s of that actor, the side without the cluster's majority refusing them with an error for the detector's window and then stopping its members (section 7) and the side with it, where it holds one of the copies, refusing them for the detector's window and the copy that the answer on a lost copy gives (below), since the detector does not tell a member across a split from a lost one: the comparison with Raft and Kafka holds for three copies, of which two are a majority, and of two copies the majority is both (the owner, 2026-10-30, "Keep 2, name the cost", against a default of three copies, two of which must take a message, as Kafka's replication factor 3 with `min.insync.replicas` 2 and a Raft group of three, at the cost of a third write to a disk and over the network for each message of every durable actor; the cost is no durable write for an actor whose copies a split separates), a cost the answer on a lost copy bounds on the side with the majority where it holds a copy. While the machine of one of an actor's two copies is lost, and the side that holds the cluster's majority holds the copy left, the actor's durable `send`s are refused until a new copy is made on another member of that side, after the detector of section 7 takes the lost member out of the log of the members, about 20 s, as Elasticsearch places a replica again after its `delayed_timeout` (the owner, 2026-10-30, "Until new copy", against a refusal while that machine is down, as Kafka with two replicas and `min.insync.replicas` 2, at the cost of writes refused until an operator acts where the machine is lost for good, and against writes to the one copy left, at the cost of "a message needs both" and of messages lost at a second failure; the cost is a copy of the actor's log over the network and onto a disk, and a rule for the member that takes it). The `send`s stay refused for the detector's 20 s and for the copy, whose time grows with the size of the actor's log. A cluster of two machines that loses one is a tie of one against one, under which the machine left stops its members (section 7) and makes no copy, while the operator's removal on a tie stands open (section 14); and what the side with the majority does with a durable actor whose copies all stand outside it is open (section 14).

### Inbox overflow

Waiting calls throttle themselves: the caller waits, so load cannot pile up. For everything else the owner's direction is that a full inbox spills into a storage engine local to the node or process, the same engine durable actors use, to free memory and queue work without cluttering everything else.

When that storage is full as well, or the target has none, the sender gets an exception. The inbox works in different modes depending on the deployment:

- `spill`: memory first, then local storage, then an exception in the sender.
- `fail`: a fixed number of slots; when they are full, an exception in the sender.
- `drop oldest`: when full, the oldest waiting message is discarded.
- `drop newest`: when full, the arriving message is discarded. *(assumed: only the name was shown to the owner)*

The default is set per deployment in `project.kz`, and an actor can override it after its name. *(assumed: the owner confirmed the modes; the placement was part of the same question)*

A waiting call that meets a full inbox raises in its caller immediately, in every mode, and `spill` takes a `send` alone; the `deploy` block sets a limit on the memory part of `spill` (the owner, 2026-10-30, "Raise + spill cap", as .NET's `BoundedChannelFullMode` and Rust's `try_send` show the full case at the write, against the modes as they stood, a waiting call dropped and left to its timeout and no limit on the memory of `spill`, at the cost of overload turned into writes to disk and stalls of 5 seconds; the cost is one more rule and one more setting). *(assumed: that the limit is the bytes the memory part of `spill` holds, at which `spill` goes on to local storage, as the mode above says, so that a limit on memory sends overload to the disk sooner and does not spare the disk, which the cost the question named for the modes as they stood does not show; and that a limit the `deploy` block sets holds for each inbox, as the default below does)*. Where the `deploy` block sets no limit, each inbox in `spill` holds up to 64 MB in memory before it goes on to local storage, as the NATS client holds up to 64 MB pending for each subscription by default (the owner, 2026-10-30, "A default limit" and "64 MB per inbox", against no limit, the unbounded memory set aside with "Raise + spill cap", and against a limit that every `deploy` block writes, at the cost of a line in each deployment and a new error id, and, for the size, against 32 MB for each inbox, at the cost of overload that reaches the disk sooner, and a quarter of the process's memory shared by all inboxes, at the cost that one actor takes the share of the others; the cost is a sum that grows with the number of actors that spill at once). The process's memory alone bounds that sum: past it an allocation that fails ends the process (section 6), every message held in memory with it.

```
// project.kz
deploy server { inbox spill }
deploy esp32  { inbox 32 fail }
```

```
actor Telemetry inbox 1000 drop oldest { }
```

### Cluster simulation tests

Required.

```
test cluster 5 seed 1337 {
    split 2 | 3
    advance 10min
    heal
    check Stock[7].Count() == 40
}
```

Clock, scheduler and network are all Kurz, so several machines run inside one process, deterministically. Any failure reproduces from its seed. C-ABI calls break the determinism.

### Record and replay

An actor is deterministic given its messages. Recording inbox and I/O results turns a crash into a file that can be stepped through. This is built for local development and testing only, not for production environments.

### Packages

```
// project.kz
use json "github.com/kurz-lang/kurz" 1.2
use mysql "github.com/example/mysql" 0.9 allow network
```

```
use json                       // may touch: nothing
use mysql allow network        // may touch: network only
```

A call through an interface on the path counts as a call of every implementer of `std/` and of the packages, and a call of a function value as a call of every such function whose value is taken, so that no grant is borrowed through them, while an implementer or a function of the program's own code is no path that needs the grant, a path from a package's call ending there and what that code calls being a path from the program's code, so that `FileLog.Write -> Store.Save -> File.Write`, with `FileLog` the program's own logger, needs the grant of `Store` and not of the package that called the logger, as the cost of the option set aside reads it (the owner, 2026-10-30, "Program's own don't count", against every implementer counting, the program's own among them, as Java's `AccessController` checks every frame of the stack, at the cost that a package that takes a logger needs `allow files` whenever the program hands it one that writes files; the cost is a rule to explain, and a walk that tells the program's code from a package's) *(assumed: that the walk counts such a call where it never reaches the function, at the cost of a refusal there; whether a `send` to an actor puts the sender's package on the path stands open, section 14)*.
